reviewer.engine: Claude subagent (read-only, images and rubric only)

views.evidence: Flower layout reads well from above. The sunflower has two rings of yellow ray petals with believable color variation, and its disk shows a phyllotaxis texture. The daisy, two lilies, coneflower and cosmos are distinct and recognizable, and the stargazer lily has convincing spots and stamens. Defects: (1) The bee on the sunflower disk (around x480-505, y290-320) is a pale beige blob about 30px across. No head, thorax and abdomen division, wings, legs or stripes can be read, so the required 'visible anatomy' check fails. (2) The ground is a blurry, low-resolution green texture with visible blocky, pixelated mottling and scattered flat grass flecks. It looks like a stretched 2D texture, not a natural ground. (3) Large soft shadows of the flowers and stems spread far to the left and are much bigger and darker than the visible plants. Several shadow silhouettes (upper left, lower left) belong to plants that are not visible, which makes the composition confusing. (4) The sunflower disk is dark brown with yellow speckles here but cream or beige in the macro and low-angle views, so the material is inconsistent between views. (5) Flowers look pasted flat onto the ground plane with almost no sense of height, apart from the shadows. Bee scale against the sunflower disk (about one fifth of its width) is plausible.

Strengths: the thorax has dense, fine, golden-brown hair with good silhouette fuzz. One forewing is thin and translucent with visible dark venation and reads as a membrane. The yellow pollen load on the hind leg is a nice touch, and the background sunflower ray petals have believable veined texture and soft depth of field. Defects: (1) The compound eyes are perfectly smooth, glossy black ellipsoids with specular highlights, like plastic beads. Real honeybee eyes are dull grey-brown with a faceted or hairy surface. (2) The antennae are straight, uniform, black cylinders with blunt cut ends and no elbow between scape and flagellum. Two of them cross awkwardly in front of the head. (3) The abdomen is a uniform tan ovoid with faint hair streaks. It lacks the honeybee's alternating dark and amber tergite bands with pale hair fringes, and the narrow waist between thorax and abdomen is not visible. (4) The legs are thin, smooth, uniform brown tubes with no hair, no tibia or tarsus taper and no visible tarsal claws. The front leg at x370-410, y570-655 ends in a point floating among the florets. (5) The second wing (upper middle, x500-690, y200-320) is a smeared, blurry, ghost-like shape that reads as a rendering artifact, not motion blur on a membrane. (6) The disk florets are identical, pale-cream bullet shapes in perfectly regular spirals with black gaps. They look like plastic pegs, not sunflower disk florets, and the cream color conflicts with the top-down view. The disk rim reads like a cream-colored bowl. Light and materials are acceptable on the petals but plasticky on the bee head and florets.

Legs traceable from body to foot: about 5 of 6. Left side: two legs (front-left foot near x345,y575 and mid-left foot near x490,y615). Right side: front-right foot near x880,y575, mid-right foot near x760,y610, and the pollen-loaded hind leg from the corbicula (x830,y440) down to about x850,y525. The left hind leg cannot be found; it is hidden behind the body. A short stub under the head (x548,y470-495) reads as mouthparts or an unclear leg fragment. Foot contacts are only partly readable. The two outer front feet appear to rest on floret tips. The two middle feet end in front of the floret field with no contact shadow or surface deformation, so they could be floating or sinking in. The pollen-loaded hind foot ends in mid-air above the disk. The legs splay out wide and long like a spider's and hold the body high above the disk. Other defects: (1) Seen head-on, the eyes are two large, glossy black lens-shaped discs glued to the sides of a black sphere. This looks cartoonish, not like a bee head. (2) Both antennae stick straight up as rigid black rods from the top of the head, with no elbow. (3) The ocelli are three small grey bumps. (4) The florets are crude, identical cones with dark voids between them that fill the lower half of the frame. (5) The background is a flat hill of grass blades under a plain sky with a hard horizon line. (6) The white lily at left looks like flat curled sheets. No obvious body-petal penetration is visible, but the bee-to-disk support is not credible.

Legs traceable from body to foot: 4 of 6. Two thoracic legs end in small two-pronged claws (x545,y720 and x740,y755). The front leg from under the head reaches about x930,y675 with a thick, blunt tip and no claw. The pollen-loaded hind leg runs from the oval pollen mesh (x465,y535) to about x440,y615. A fifth limb is a horizontal cylinder (x480-585, y490-505) that sticks out sideways from under the abdomen, ends in a flat, capped stump and does not reach any surface. It reads as a detached or misplaced hind femur. A sixth short segment near x850-920, y540-590 under the head cannot be traced to a foot. Foot contacts: the two clawed feet appear to sit on top of the dark floret field, but the depth relationship is ambiguous. The front foot (x930,y675) and the pollen hind foot (x440,y615) end in mid-air. Mesh problems: (1) The antenna cylinders pass straight through the head mesh (x880-1055, y345-410) with no socket; this is a visible interpenetration. (2) The abdomen ellipsoid (left, white) overlaps the thorax sphere with no petiole or waist geometry, so it is an obvious primitive intersection. (3) The legs are low-segment straight cylinders with abrupt joints and no taper. (4) The eye ellipsoids are separate primitives stuck onto the head. (5) The raised wing (x640-830, y140-310) shows coarse, irregular internal triangles and duplicated vein loops; the left forewing mesh is clean and long. (6) The hair shell is a dense point or line cloud on the thorax that is fine at this scale. The petals and florets are well tessellated, with no abnormal stretching on the flower.

blockers: low_angle_anti_clip: six-leg support cannot be verified. At most 5 legs can be traced, the left hind leg is hidden, and the pollen hind foot plus at least two other feet end in mid-air or have ambiguous contact with the disk. The required six-leg contact assessment fails.

wireframe: the antenna cylinders visibly pass through the head mesh, and a hind-leg cylinder sticks out horizontally from under the abdomen as a detached, capped stump. These are obvious intersection and continuity defects.
top_down: the bee is an unreadable pale blob at this framing and resolution, so the required 'visible anatomy' and bee/flower assessment cannot be made credibly.
repairs: P1 Leg rig and contacts: rebuild all six legs as tapered coxa-trochanter-femur-tibia-tarsus chains attached to the thorax underside, in the correct order (fore, mid, hind). Use IK so every one of the six tarsi plants on the actual floret-top surface, with tarsal claws and a small contact shadow or occlusion. Remove the stray horizontal hind-leg cylinder under the abdomen and put the pollen-loaded hind leg on the thorax with its foot on the disk. Lower the body so the stance is compact, not spider-like.

P1 Head: replace the glossy black eye ellipsoids with dull grey-brown faceted (normal-mapped), slightly hairy compound eyes blended into the head capsule. Build elbowed (geniculate) antennae that start from sockets on the face and do not pass through the head mesh; taper the flagellum.

P1 Abdomen: model the narrow petiole and waist between thorax and abdomen so the primitives no longer overlap visibly. Add segmented tergites with alternating dark-brown and amber bands and pale hair fringes typical of Apis mellifera.

P2 Wings: fix the blurry, smeared second wing so both forewings and hindwings render as crisp, thin, translucent veined membranes, or use a proper, consistent motion-blur treatment. Clean up the irregular triangulation on the raised wing.

P2 Sunflower disk: replace the identical pale-cream bullet florets with varied disk florets (darker brown or purple toward the center, open yellow florets at the rim, size gradient, jitter). Fill the black voids with a base receptacle surface, and make the disk color match across views.

P2 Top-down readability: make sure the bee is legible from above (adequate size or contrast, wing and stripe silhouette, a contact shadow on the disk). Replace the blocky, pixelated ground texture with a higher-resolution, natural soil or grass surface, and reconcile oversized shadows from off-screen plants with what is visible.
P3 Legs and materials: add fine hair to legs and abdomen, reduce specular gloss on the chitin, and add a corbicula pollen texture that sits on the hind tibia, not hanging off it.
P3 Environment: soften the hard horizon and flat grass hill in the low-angle view, and add thickness and curvature shading to the lily petals so they do not read as flat sheets.
